newsitem.title: USA: US West Coast crudes up with WTI, but trading thin.
newsitem.headline: US West Coast crudes up with WTI, but trading thin.

text.p: U.S. West Coast crude prices rose with benchmark grades Wednesday, amid news that Canadian imports were unchanged, despite pipeline shutdowns which could have sent excess crude to Northwest refiners.
In Canada, two shut pipelines on IPL Energy's pipeline into the U.S. began flowing at low rates Tuesday after power was restored to two pumping stations in the U.S. Midwest.
Trans Mountain Pipe line, which carries excess crude from Canada to Northwest refineries, said ample tank space allowed producers to store crude in Canada rather than export it.
"There was some increase in nominations, but nothing significant," said a pipeline official.
West Coast refiners hoped extra Canadian supplies would be sold at a strong discount.
Meanwhile, West Coast crude buyers were angered by a rumor that BP secretly sold a second cargo of Alaska North Slope (ANS) crude last week at a discount wider than $1.05, the current posted price.
BP and Exxon denied selling the cargo, but U.S. Oil, the alleged buyer, declined to comment when asked if they purchased the crude.
Outright ANS rose 30 cents to $18.53/18.73 a barrel.

One refinery trader said U.S. Oil declined their offer of Colombian South Blend crude because they had bought the cargo of ANS. The trader said U.S. Oil could have bought the cargo at $1.10 below WTI or wider.
A 2,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) shipment for California heavy grade in May sold at postings Tuesday, traders said.
